concepts.title: Computer Networks and Protocols
concepts.summary: Networks connect computing devices via copper, fibre, or radio to exchange data, governed by agreed-upon rules called protocols.
concepts.explanation: A computer network is formed when two or more computing devices join together to share resources and exchange data. The physical medium can be wired (copper or fibre) or wireless (radio waves). To ensure devices can understand one another across different hardware and software configurations, they use protocols, which are mutually agreed-upon sets of rules defining message formats and behaviors.
concepts.sourceExcerpt: A computer network is two or more computing devices joined togetherto exchange data and share resources. The devices may be wired withcopper or fibre, or joined wirelessly over radio. A protocol is anagreed set of rules that lets two devices understand each other.
keyPoints: Networks connect devices to share data and resources.
Physical connections can be wired (copper/fibre) or wireless (radio).
Protocols provide agreed rules for device communication.
concepts.whyItMatters: Without protocols and network connectivity, modern digital communication, internet browsing, and distributed computing would be impossible.
concepts.analogy: Protocols are like human languages; two people from different regions need to agree on a common language (like English) to successfully converse.

explanationLevels.simple: Computers linked together to share files, talking to each other using shared rules.
explanationLevels.everyday: Just like office workers sharing a printer over an office router and following standard email formats, computers follow strict rules to talk.
explanationLevels.advanced: A distributed system of autonomous nodes interconnected via physical transmission media, operating under standardized multi-layer protocol stacks.

concepts.commonTrap: Assuming wireless networks do not require physical infrastructure.
concepts.correctiveTruth: Wireless devices still connect to physical access points and routers that interface with wired backbones.

comparison.takeaway: Wired offers speed and security; wireless offers mobility.

rows.second: Susceptible to obstacles and signal interference

concepts.originStory: Early computer networks like ARPANET were developed in the late 1960s to allow researchers to share expensive computing resources remotely.

concepts.title: TCP/IP Model and Handshake
concepts.summary: The TCP/IP model has four abstraction layers, and TCP connection establishment relies on a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
concepts.explanation: The TCP/IP model organizes network functionality into four layers, where each layer adds services for the layer above and hides lower-level implementation details. To establish a reliable connection, TCP uses a three-way handshake: the client sends a SYN packet, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client acknowledges with ACK.
concepts.sourceExcerpt: The TCP/IP model has four layers. Each layer adds a service for thelayer above it and hides how the lower layers work... The TCP handshake is a three-step exchange. The client sends SYN, theserver replies SYN-ACK, and the client answers with ACK.
keyPoints: TCP/IP model consists of four layers.
Each layer encapsulates data and hides lower layer complexity.
concepts.whyItMatters: The three-way handshake ensures both sender and receiver are ready and synchronized before data transmission begins.
concepts.analogy: A phone call: Person A calls (SYN), Person B answers and says hello (SYN-ACK), Person A acknowledges and starts talking (ACK).

explanationLevels.simple: A four-level system where computers agree to talk before sending data.
explanationLevels.everyday: Like knocking on a door, hearing 'Who is it?', replying 'It's me', and having the door opened.
explanationLevels.advanced: A four-tier protocol stack utilizing sequence number synchronization via a three-way handshake to establish stateful transport connections.

concepts.commonTrap: Assuming data can be sent immediately without establishing a connection.
concepts.correctiveTruth: TCP requires a completed three-way handshake before application data flows.

comparison.takeaway: Handshake steps progress from request to final confirmation.

concepts.originStory: Developed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the 1970s, TCP/IP became the foundational architecture of the modern Internet.

concepts.title: Switching and MAC Address Tables
concepts.summary: Ethernet switches use MAC address tables learned dynamically from incoming frames to forward data, flooding unknown destinations.
concepts.explanation: An Ethernet switch directs frames across a local network using a MAC address table. Each port learns which MAC address is connected behind it by inspecting the source address of incoming frames. If a destination address is not found in the table, the switch floods the frame to every port except the arrival port.
concepts.sourceExcerpt: An Ethernet switch forwards frames using a MAC address table. Eachport learns which MAC address sits behind it by watching the sourceaddress of arriving frames. A frame for an unknown address is floodedto every port except the one it arrived on.
keyPoints: Switches use MAC address tables to forward frames.
Ports learn MAC addresses from arriving source headers.
Unknown destination addresses trigger flooding to all other ports.
concepts.whyItMatters: Switching allows efficient point-to-point communication on local area networks without broadcasting every packet to all devices.
concepts.analogy: A mailroom sorting clerk who looks at the return address on incoming letters to remember desk locations, and asks around if a recipient is unknown.

explanationLevels.simple: A smart splitter that learns where computers are plugged in.
explanationLevels.everyday: Like a receptionist keeping a log of who sits in which office chair based on who walks through which door.
explanationLevels.advanced: Layer 2 data-link forwarding mechanism utilizing content-addressable memory (CAM) tables and destination-based filtering.

concepts.commonTrap: Assuming switches broadcast every frame to all devices like old hubs do.
concepts.correctiveTruth: Switches forward frames directly to the target port once the MAC address is learned.

comparison.takeaway: Switches optimize known traffic and flood unknown traffic.

rows.first: Forwarded only to the specific target port
rows.second: Flooded to all ports except ingress port

concepts.originStory: Ethernet switching replaced shared broadcast hubs in the 1990s, dramatically increasing LAN bandwidth and reducing collisions.

concepts.title: IP Addressing and Subnetting
concepts.summary: IP addresses are hierarchical, using routers with TTL fields and subnet masks to divide network and host portions.
concepts.explanation: IP addressing uses hierarchical structures where routers strip network prefixes to route packets to the next hop. A Time to Live (TTL) field decrements at each router to prevent infinite loops. Subnet masks divide the IP address into network and host portions; for example, a /24 mask leaves the final octet for hosts, providing 254 usable addresses.
concepts.sourceExcerpt: IP addressing is hierarchical. A router strips the network portion ofthe destination address and forwards the packet to the next hop. TheTime to Live field decreases by one at every router, preventing loops... Subnet masks decide where the network number ends and the host numberbegins. A /24 mask reserves the final octet for hosts, giving 254usable addresses...
keyPoints: IP addressing is hierarchical to enable scalable routing.
TTL field prevents packets from looping infinitely.
Subnet masks separate network and host portions (e.g., /24 gives 254 usable host addresses).
concepts.whyItMatters: Subnetting and hierarchical routing allow the global Internet to manage billions of devices efficiently without catastrophic routing table bloat.
concepts.analogy: Postal addresses: Country -> State -> City -> Street -> House Number, where the router acts as a postal hub sorting mail by region.

explanationLevels.simple: Organized house numbers that help mail carriers find the right neighborhood and street.
explanationLevels.everyday: Like phone numbers split into country code, area code, and local subscriber number.
explanationLevels.advanced: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) architecture utilizing bitwise subnet masks and decrementing hop-limit counters for loop prevention.

concepts.commonTrap: Assuming all IP addresses in a subnet are assignable to hosts.
concepts.correctiveTruth: Network and broadcast addresses are reserved, reducing usable host IPs by two.

comparison.takeaway: Subnet masks divide IP addresses into routing prefix and local device identifier.

rows.second: Identifies the individual device on the network

concepts.originStory: IPv4 was standardized in the early 1980s, and CIDR was introduced in 1993 to combat IPv4 address exhaustion.

concepts.title: TCP Congestion Control and Reliability
concepts.summary: TCP congestion control uses slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and dynamic retransmission timers to maintain efficiency.
concepts.explanation: Congestion control keeps networks efficient and prevents senders from flooding links. TCP utilizes four phases: slow start (doubling the sending window per round trip), congestion avoidance (growing the window linearly), fast retransmit (resending missing segments after three duplicate ACKs), and fast recovery. Additionally, retransmission timers balance timeout values using dynamic round-trip time estimates.
concepts.sourceExcerpt: Congestion control has two main goals: keep the network efficient andkeep any one sender from flooding the links it shares. The four phasesof TCP congestion control are slow start, congestion avoidance, fastretransmit and fast recovery... Retransmission timers must balance two failure modes. A timer set toolow triggers needless resends and wastes bandwidth. A timer set toohigh leaves a gap in the connection.
keyPoints: Congestion control maintains efficiency and prevents link flooding.
Four phases: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery.
Retransmission timers use dynamic RTT estimates to avoid premature timeouts or lag.
concepts.whyItMatters: Without congestion control, high traffic volumes would cause network collapses, massive packet loss, and severe connection sluggishness.
concepts.analogy: Driving in traffic: speeding up carefully on clear roads (slow start), maintaining steady acceleration (congestion avoidance), and slowing down immediately when brake lights appear.

explanationLevels.simple: Rules that tell computers to slow down when the network gets too busy.
explanationLevels.everyday: Like adjusting your highway driving speed based on traffic density so you don't cause a pileup.
explanationLevels.advanced: Additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) congestion window algorithms coupled with adaptive round-trip time estimators.

concepts.commonTrap: Assuming slow start keeps sending slowly throughout the entire connection.
concepts.correctiveTruth: Slow start exponentially doubles the window size rapidly until packet loss or a threshold is reached.

comparison.takeaway: Window growth transitions from exponential to linear as network limits approach.

rows.second: Grows by one segment per round trip (linear)

concepts.originStory: Van Jacobson introduced TCP congestion control algorithms in 1988, preventing widespread Internet congestion collapses.
